title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 5: Nominating the Best and the Brightest
keywords: Nominating the Best and the Brightest
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's account, as ex-officio chairperson of the Judicial and Bar Council, of how he is reforming judicial entry so that the JBC nominates 'the best and the brightest' rather than merely processing whoever applies.

The three Ss framework he imposed on the Council -- search for, screen and select -- with the first S, an activist nationwide search, added on his initiative because the JBC had previously done only the second and third.

The four Ins (integrity, independence, industry and intelligence) as the entry standard, argued to matter even more for new entrants than for incumbents, since contaminated inflow permanently muddies the judicial reservoir.

A defense of the JBC against critics who would abolish it and return to presidential appointment with Commission on Appointments confirmation, coupled with his admission that the Council must become more proactive, transparent, assertive and accountable.
sub_topics: The February 11, 2005 invitation from his 'revered guru' former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga to address Bantay Katarungan's fifth anniversary and the Kilosbayan forum, where he spoke on 'Judging the Judges.'

The constitutional attributes of a magistrate -- competence, integrity, probity and independence -- and the seven attributes of the New Code of Judicial Conduct effective June 1, 2004, which he compresses into the four Ins.
His argument that entry standards matter most: cleansing the judiciary of the errant is less urgent than keeping muddy water out of the judicial reservoir.
His convening of the JBC in his first official days of January 2006 to review its mission, processes, effectiveness, restrictions and public criticisms.

The three Ss and the constitutional design of the JBC: at least three nominees per vacancy, appointments exempt from Commission on Appointments confirmation to forestall partisan politics, citing the UN Declaration of Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary.

The wider search: nationwide dialogues with the bar, justice agencies, the academe, NGOs, media, civic groups and the public; radio and television public service announcements; and a JBC website launched April 21, 2006 and hyperlinked to the Supreme Court's.

The compressed timetable forced by the constitutional 90-day deadline for the Supreme Court vacancy created by CJ Davide's retirement and his own ascension on December 20, 2005, limiting dialogues to the IBP, PBA and Wiloci, the Society for Judicial Excellence, and the media.

Incentives the JBC will advertise to attract applicants: the phased 100-percent increase in judicial pay from 2003, easing of workload as vacancies are filled, the new Supreme Court Security Committee under Justice Cancio C. Garcia, and better halls of justice including Guagua, Iloilo City and the old GSIS building on Arroceros Street.

The vacancy problem: 28.86 percent of 2,152 authorized trial court positions vacant, against about 32 percent and 29.49 percent earlier, with promotion of judges and a one-year-three-month filling process as the causes, and first-level rural and peace-and-order-troubled courts worst affected.

The scheduling fix: announcing vacancies and accepting applications three months before compulsory retirements, submitting nominees on the day the vacancy arises, and asking the President to appoint within 90 days, aiming to halve the vacancy rate.

More thorough and transparent screening: qualifications, background investigations, psychological and psychiatric examinations, personal interviews, and interviews opened to the public for the ombudsman and the appellate and Supreme Court posts.

Screening criteria by category -- track record, administrative cases, bar ratings, publications and speeches; for judges, length of service, quality of decisions and speed of disposition; for prosecutors and practitioners, cases won and lost and quality of pleadings.
Background investigation capacity: the NBI's delays from insufficient personnel despite 95 percent positive reports, and the Council's plan to hire 12 investigators of its own.
Disqualifications under the JBC Rules for serious pending criminal or administrative cases and for convictions carrying a fine above P10,000.

The February 14-16 interviews of 14 candidates for the lone Supreme Court vacancy, attended by Bantay Katarungan monitors whose written questions Justice Raoul V. Victorino put to applicants and openly attributed to them.

Selection by secret ballot subject to the 'integrity vote' under Section 2 of Rule 10, which disqualifies a candidate on the negative vote of a single member on integrity, plus a proposed point system for ranking.
His appeal to endorsers, especially politicians, to refrain from recommending the undeserving, and his assessment of endorsements by the credibility and closeness of the endorser.

His institutional defense: the JBC is a 1987 Philippine innovation now copied abroad, sits in Article VIII under the supervision of the Supreme Court, and operates by judicial rather than partisan legislative process.

stances.claim: Entry standards matter more than discipline: it is even more necessary to ensure that a new entrant possesses the four Ins than to cleanse the judiciary of the errant, because contaminated inflow permanently fouls the judicial reservoir.
stances.rhetorical_move: reservoir metaphor carrying the argument -- muddy inflow makes cleansing futile, so screening at entry is the higher priority

stances.claim: The JBC must do three things, not two: search as well as screen and select, because the Council cannot recruit the best and the brightest if the pool it filters is neither wide nor deep enough.
stances.rhetorical_move: mnemonic triad plus rhetorical question, then report of the concrete reforms he had the Council adopt

stances.claim: The Judicial and Bar Council should not be abolished in favor of presidential appointment confirmed by the Commission on Appointments, because the JBC is a Philippine innovation now copied abroad and belongs to the Judicial Department, operating by a somber judicial process rather than partisan legislative slinging.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering critics on their own ground -- conceding the need for reform while defending the institution's constitutional placement and comparative pedigree

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' recorded how Chief Justice Panganiban, as ex-officio chairperson of the Judicial and Bar Council, set out to reform judicial entry. He began by recalling the February 11, 2005 occasion when his revered guru, former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, summoned him to address Bantay Katarungan and Kilosbayan on 'Judging the Judges,' where he compressed the Constitution's four attributes of a magistrate and the seven attributes of the 2004 New Code of Judicial Conduct into four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence. Those standards, he argued, matter even more at entry than in discipline, since the water of the judicial reservoir will always be murky if the inflow carries the germs of incompetence, indifference, influence and indolence. On his first official days in January 2006 he convened the Council to review its mission, effectiveness and public criticisms, and framed its work as three Ss -- search for, screen and select. The JBC had previously done only the last two; on his initiative it added an activist search through nationwide dialogues with the bar, justice agencies, the academe, NGOs, media and the public, radio and television announcements, and a website launched April 21, 2006. Constitutional deadlines for the Supreme Court vacancy left by Chief Justice Davide's retirement compressed that program, so dialogues were limited to the IBP, PBA, Wiloci, the Society for Judicial Excellence and the media. He detailed the incentives the Council would advertise -- doubled judicial pay, a new Security Committee, better halls of justice -- and the vacancy statistics driving the urgency, along with a new practice of announcing vacancies three months before retirements. Screening, he reported, now included background investigations, psychological and psychiatric examinations and public interviews, with selection by secret ballot subject to the integrity vote under Rule 10. He closed by defending the JBC against calls for its abolition while conceding it must become more proactive, transparent, assertive and accountable.
